subject: Physics
scope: 16 original AQA AS Physics Electricity mock recall cards, focused on selected subtleties after reviewing existing coverage.
notes: No claim of exhaustive 3.5 specification sign-off. Theory and graphs only; no practical apparatus setup instructions. Original historic IDs and progress remain unchanged.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In a metal wire, how does electron drift direction compare with conventional current direction?
cards.back: Electrons drift opposite to conventional current.
accept: Electrons drift opposite to conventional current.
The electron movement is opposite the direction of conventional current.
Electron drift is from the negative end towards the positive end, whereas conventional current is opposite.
reject: Electrons drift in the same direction as conventional current.
No charge carriers move in a conducting wire.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For an ohmic resistor held at constant temperature, what shape is its current–potential-difference graph?
cards.back: A straight line through the origin.
accept: A straight line through the origin.
A linear I–V characteristic passing through (0, 0).
Current is proportional to potential difference.
reject: A curved line that becomes flatter as current increases.
A straight line that always has a non-zero current-axis intercept.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a non-ohmic component, can resistance at a chosen I–V graph point generally be found from the tangent gradient?
cards.back: No. Calculate R = V/I using the coordinates of the point; tangent gradient is not generally V/I.
accept: No. Calculate R = V/I using the coordinates of the point; tangent gradient is not generally V/I.
Use V divided by I at the point rather than a tangent gradient.
The resistance at an operating point is potential difference divided by current, not the I–V tangent slope.
reject: Yes, every tangent gradient on I against V is the resistance.
Resistance always equals dI/dV.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A metal wire's resistance rises with temperature while an NTC thermistor's resistance falls. What is the contrasting trend?
cards.back: Metal resistance increases; NTC thermistor resistance decreases as temperature rises.
accept: Metal resistance increases; NTC thermistor resistance decreases as temperature rises.
The metal has a positive temperature trend and the NTC thermistor a negative one.
Metals usually gain resistance on heating, NTC thermistors lose resistance.
reject: Both resistances decrease with rising temperature.
Both resistances stay constant as temperature changes.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can an NTC semiconductor thermistor become less resistive as it warms?
cards.back: Heating increases the number of mobile charge carriers, which can reduce its resistance.
accept: Heating increases the number of mobile charge carriers, which can reduce its resistance.
More charge carriers become available at higher temperature.
Higher temperature releases more mobile carriers, making the NTC thermistor more conducting.
reject: It becomes an ideal superconductor whenever warmed.
Its resistance must increase because it is identical to a metal.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Uniform wire: R–length graph gradient m, cross-section A. Find resistivity ρ.
accept: ρ = mA.
Resistivity equals the resistance-length gradient multiplied by cross-sectional area.
rho is gradient times A.
reject: ρ = m/A.
ρ = A/m.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of the gradient of an R-against-L graph, and what unit results after multiplying by area?
cards.back: Gradient: Ω m⁻¹; resistivity: Ω m.
accept: Gradient: Ω m⁻¹; resistivity: Ω m.
Ohms per metre for gradient, ohm metres for resistivity.
Gradient is resistance per length; multiplying by m squared gives ohm metre.
reject: Gradient is Ω m and resistivity is Ω m⁻¹.
Gradient is amperes per metre and resistivity is volts.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For an otherwise uniform wire, what might a non-zero positive R-intercept on an R-against-L graph indicate?
cards.back: Extra contact or lead resistance that is approximately independent of the measured wire length.
accept: Extra contact or lead resistance that is approximately independent of the measured wire length.
Constant contact resistance can cause a positive intercept.
The measured resistance contains a fixed contribution from connections or leads.
reject: It proves the wire's resistivity is zero.
It means the wire's resistance cannot depend on length.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A wire's measured diameter has a 2% uncertainty. Approximately what is the percentage uncertainty in its calculated area?
cards.back: 4%, because cross-sectional area is proportional to diameter squared.
accept: 4%, because cross-sectional area is proportional to diameter squared.
Approximately four per cent.
Twice the diameter percentage uncertainty, giving 4 percent.
reject: 2%, because diameter and area are directly proportional.
1%, because squaring halves the uncertainty.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: If the diameter of a uniform wire doubles with material, length and temperature fixed, what happens to its resistance?
cards.back: It becomes one quarter of its original resistance.
accept: It becomes one quarter of its original resistance.
Resistance is quartered.
The cross-sectional area quadruples so resistance decreases by a factor of four.
reject: Resistance doubles.
Resistance increases fourfold.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: At fixed potential difference across a resistor, what happens to electrical power if resistance doubles?
accept: Power halves because P = V²/R.
Power becomes one half.
At constant voltage power is inversely proportional to resistance.
reject: Power doubles.
Power stays the same.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: At fixed current through a resistor, what happens to electrical power if resistance doubles?
accept: Power doubles because P = I²R.
Power becomes twice the original.
At constant current dissipated power is proportional to resistance.
reject: Power halves.
Power stays the same.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Divider: load RL is across the lower resistor R2. What effective lower resistance do you use?
cards.back: Rlower = R2RL/(R2 + RL), the parallel combination.
accept: Rlower = R2RL/(R2 + RL), the parallel combination.
Use the parallel equivalent of R2 and RL.
The lower resistance becomes one over (one over R2 plus one over RL).
reject: Use R2 + RL.
Ignore the load when calculating the output.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can connecting a measuring load across the lower divider resistor reduce the output p.d.?
cards.back: The load acts in parallel with that resistor, reducing the effective lower resistance and its share of the supply voltage.
accept: The load acts in parallel with that resistor, reducing the effective lower resistance and its share of the supply voltage.
The bottom branch equivalent resistance falls, so Vout decreases.
The load draws current and reduces the fraction of supply potential difference across the lower part.
reject: The lower effective resistance always increases.
The supply emf must necessarily increase when a load is attached.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Cell with internal resistance r and current I: rate of internal energy loss?
accept: P_lost = I²r.
Power loss in the cell is current squared times internal resistance.
The internal heating power is I times lost volts, I²r.
reject: P_lost = Ir, in watts.
Power lost is always zero for a real cell.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Two identical cells in parallel (emf ε, internal r each) feed load R. Find current I.
accept: Current equals emf divided by load resistance plus half the internal resistance.
I is epsilon over R plus r divided by 2, with the whole sum as denominator.
